name: The Time Machine
lines: The Time Machine: Richmond, and the year 802,701
Richmond, the Time Traveller's house
The Further Vision
the road outside, at Richmond
the fireside in the smoking-room
the little octagonal table
the Time Machine, in the laboratory
the garden behind the house
the lawn of the White Sphinx
the bronze panels of the pedestal
the rhododendrons round the lawn
the great hall of the Eloi
the carved doorway of the great hall
inside the great hall, among the tables
the hill-top, and the seat of yellow metal
the seat of yellow metal
the river's edge, where the Eloi bathe
the great ruined building
inside the ruin, in the shadows
a well, with its little cupola
the well by the ruins
a well on the slope
a well among the trees
a tall tower, its top breathing air
the edge of the great wood
a glade in the wood
the knoll where you slept the first night
the Palace of Green Porcelain
the great broken valves of the door
the Gallery of Palaeontology
the gallery of minerals
the gallery of great machines
the machine with the lever
the dark end of the gallery of machines
the gallery of rotting books
the gallery of technical chemistry
the stands of rusting arms
the little turfed court with three fruit-trees
the burnt wood, and the hill beyond
the foot of the shaft
the great cavern of machines
the table in the cavern
the shore under the red sun
the slope of the beach
the beach, thirty million years on
The Time Traveller
Ah, there you are. Sit down, sit down. You must follow me carefully: I shall have to controvert one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted.
I'm starving for a bit of meat. Don't ask me any questions yet: let me tell it my own way.
Good evening. You have come to see his latest paradox, I suppose?
Evening. He looks well, at least: a touch of fever about the eyes, perhaps.
The Provincial Mayor
Ah. How d'ye do. Clever fellow, our host. Too clever by half, if you ask me.
I don't believe a word of it, and I shall say so. That reminds me of a conjuror I once saw at Burslem...
The Very Young Man
I say! Have you heard? He says he can travel in time! Think of the investments!
Evening. Where's our host? Late again, I suppose.
Evening! Any copy in it tonight, do you think?
(He nods, and smiles shyly.)
Good evening, sir. The master's in the laboratory again, I don't doubt.
(She laughs, and puts a flower into your hand.)
an Eloi with flowers
an Eloi in a purple tunic
a little Eloi girl
(Soft, sweet, liquid words, and a peal of laughter.)
(A garland of flowers is dropped round your neck, with a laugh.)
(Bright eyes, a quick question in a cooing voice, and then they lose interest and drift away.)
(They point at the sun, and then at you, and ask, in their gentle way: did you come from the sun?)
(A fruit is put into your hand: a sort of floury thing in a three-sided husk.)
(A yawn, a smile, and they wander off among the flowers.)

a lady of Richmond

Good evening. A fine evening for it.
Evening. Lights in the clever gentleman's laboratory again, I see.
Good evening to you.
Evening. Mind the puddle there.
Mr. Hartley, a stockbroker
Come in, come in. You're from the house with the brass lamp? Your friend's laboratory hums all night, you know. My wife swears she saw a light go clean through the wall.
Mrs. Pell, a widow
Good evening. Do sit down; the kettle is on. I keep the parlour as my husband liked it.
Dr. Sheen, a retired surgeon
Evening. I keep my old instruments in that cabinet, and read the Lancet by the fire. What brings you?
Miss Ada Crane, a governess
Oh! Good evening. The children are in bed at last. Mind the dolls' house.
Mr. Bolt, an engineer
Evening. Dynamos, sir, are the coming thing. Electric light in every house on this road within ten years, you mark me.
Mrs. Dacre, a painter
Come in, but mind the wet canvas. I paint the river at Richmond every morning in a different light.
Mr. Lamb, a curate
Good evening, good evening. I am writing Sunday's sermon, on the lilies of the field.
The Misses Grey, two sisters
Good evening! Will you take a cup of tea? Sister plays the piano after supper, if you care to stay.
Mr. Fenn, a bookseller
Evening. Every book in this house I have read twice. Mr. Wells? No, I don't know the name.
a child of the house
Good evening! I'm allowed up till nine.

The Time Traveller's after-dinner argument

Richmond, Surrey, the 1890s, a Thursday evening after dinner. You are one of the Time Traveller's guests, in his smoking-room, with the Psychologist, the Medical Man, the Provincial Mayor, Filby, and a very young man. The fire is bright. He is about to tell you that time is only a fourth dimension of space.
The smoking-room, after dinner
The Time Traveller, by the fire: listen to him
The fire burnt brightly, and the soft radiance of the incandescent lights in the lilies of silver caught the bubbles that flashed and passed in our glasses.
You must follow me carefully. I shall have to controvert one or two ideas that are almost universally accepted.
Filby, "an argumentative person with red hair", objects
Of course a solid body may exist. All real things—
So most people think. But wait a moment. Can an instantaneous cube exist?
"Clearly," says the Time Traveller, "any real body must have extension in four directions." Length, breadth, thickness... and what is the fourth?
Weight is not a direction one can travel in.
Colour? He smiles: no.
it must have Length, Breadth, Thickness, and—Duration.
The Provincial Mayor has never heard of the fourth dimension
It is simply this. That Space, as our mathematicians have it, is spoken of as having three dimensions, which one may call Length, Breadth, and Thickness
The Medical Man stares at a coal in the fire: why can we not move in time?
🩺 The great difficulty
why cannot we move in Time as we move about in the other dimensions of Space?
Are you so sure we can move freely in Space?
There are balloons.
The Time Traveller asks: which way are we NOT free to move in space, before balloons were made?
Backward and forward
We go left and right freely enough.
Backward and forward, freely enough.
🎈 Gravitation limits us there. And in time, he says, we are always moving, "from the cradle to the grave".
The Very Young Man has an idea
To travel through Time!
Then there is the future,
One might invest all one’s money, leave it to accumulate at interest, and hurry on ahead!
The Psychologist: "it's all humbug"
Let’s see your experiment anyhow,
though it’s all humbug, you know.

The Time Traveller smiled round at us. Then, still smiling faintly, and with his hands deep in his trousers pockets, he walked slowly out of the room, and we heard his slippers shuffling down the long passage to his laboratory.
I wonder what he’s got?
Some sleight-of-hand trick or other,
Wait by the little octagonal table for him to come back (Filby is telling a story about a conjuror)

The thing the Time Traveller held in his hand was a glittering metallic framework, scarcely larger than a small clock, and very delicately made. There was ivory in it, and some transparent crystalline substance.
Look at the little model on the octagonal table
✨ A little framework of brass and ivory and twisted quartz, with a tiny saddle and two tiny levers. One bar twinkles oddly, as though it were not quite real.
He asks the Psychologist to lend him a hand
👉 Lend me your hand
this lever, being pressed over, sends the machine gliding into the future, and this other reverses the motion.
Lend me your hand.
▶ The Psychologist presses the lever
💨 There is a breath of wind. The lamp flame jumps. The little machine swings round, becomes indistinct, is seen as a ghost for a second... and is gone.
💨 Where did it go?
Everyone is silent. Then Filby says he is damned. The Psychologist looks under the table. Where does the Time Traveller say the little machine has gone?
Under the table, by a trick
Into the future or the past: he does not know which
Into the laboratory
The Psychologist has looked: it is not there.
It has not moved in space at all, he says.
Into the future or the past—I don’t, for certain, know which.
The Psychologist explains why you cannot see it
🌀 The spoke of a wheel
We cannot see it, nor can we appreciate this machine, any more than we can the spoke of a wheel spinning, or a bullet flying through the air.
🌀 Why can't we see it?
If the model is travelling through time fifty or a hundred times faster than we are, why can none of you see it on the table?
It is invisible glass
It passes each moment too quickly to be seen, like a spinning spoke
The lamp is too dim
It was brass and ivory a minute ago.
Turn up the lamp: still nothing.
🌀 Presentation below the threshold, the Psychologist calls it. Diluted presentation.
The lamp held up over the Time Machine
"Would you like to see the Time Machine itself?" He takes the lamp and leads you all down the long, draughty corridor to his laboratory.
Down the corridor to the laboratory
Out into the hall, after the lamp
Down the long, draughty corridor to the laboratory
Look at the Machine itself
⏳ Nickel and ivory, brass and twisted rods of rock crystal; a saddle; two levers before it; and four small dials. Parts of it are clearly not finished: on the bench lie rods of quartz, half filed.
The Medical Man: "are you perfectly serious?"
are you perfectly serious? Or is this a trick—like that ghost you showed us last Christmas?
Upon that machine,
I intend to explore time. Is that plain? I was never more serious in my life.

Four small dials stand before the saddle. The Time Traveller explains them: one for days, one for thousands of days, one for millions, one for thousands of millions. To go 1,000 days ahead, which dial moves round once?
The thousands of days, one step only; the days dial goes round once
It does more than move: it goes all the way round, once, and hands on to the next.
Far too far: that would be centuries.
⏳ Right: a thousand days turn the first dial right round and move the second on one.
Filby, over the Medical Man's shoulder
None of us quite knew how to take it.
I caught Filby’s eye over the shoulder of the Medical Man, and he winked at me solemnly.
The Psychologist thinks it over
None of you quite believe it. "The fact is, the Time Traveller was one of those men who are too clever to be believed." Will you come again next Thursday? Of course you will.
Back to the hall: it is late, and time to go home
Out into the road; the cabs wait under the gas lamps
The Time Traveller Returns
His plate of mutton

The next Thursday. You go again to Richmond, and arrive late. Four or five men are already in the drawing-room. The Medical Man is standing before the fire with a note in one hand and his watch in the other. Your host is not there.
Richmond, next Thursday, seven o'clock
In at the front door; the hall lamp is lit
Into the drawing-room, where the others wait
The Medical Man has a note from your host
He’s unavoidably detained. He asks me in this note to lead off with dinner at seven if he’s not back. Says he’ll explain when he comes.
It seems a pity to let the dinner spoil,
The Editor of a well-known daily paper
The Editor is a rare visitor: worldly and quick. He thinks your host's time-travelling is a fine paradox and a better joke.
A quiet, shy man with a beard
a quiet, shy man with a beard—whom I didn’t know, and who, as far as my observation went, never opened his mouth all the evening.
Into the dining-room: dinner at seven, without him
Sit at the table while the soup goes round
The door from the corridor opens slowly. Who is it?
Mrs. Watchett, with the fish
The Time Traveller, in an amazing plight
Not Mrs. Watchett.
He was in an amazing plight. His coat was dusty and dirty, and smeared with green down the sleeves; his hair disordered, and as it seemed to me greyer
Look at him: haggard, limping, a cut on his chin
He said not a word, but came painfully to the table, and made a motion towards the wine.
I’m—funny! Be all right in a minute.
▶ He goes upstairs to wash
As he goes out, you stand up and see his feet. What has he on them?
Only a pair of tattered, stained socks
Not even slippers.
🧦 Nothing but a pair of tattered, stained socks. Where can he have been?
The Journalist: "what's the game?"
🎩 What's the game?
Has he been doing the Amateur Cadger? I don’t follow.
Wait at the table: the dinner goes on, uneasily
He comes back, washed and changed
🍖 Where's my mutton?
Where’s my mutton?
What a treat it is to stick a fork into meat again!
